 Rhodium metal–rhodium oxide (Rh–Rh2O3)
Published on 25 October 2018. Downloaded by The University of Tokyo on 1/15/2026 8:51:22 AM.

 Cite this: J. Mater. Chem. A, 2018, 6,
 nanostructures with Pt-like or better activity
 23531 towards hydrogen evolution and oxidation
 reactions (HER, HOR) in acid and base: correlating
 its HOR/HER activity with hydrogen binding energy
 and oxophilicity of the catalyst†
 Manas Kumar Kundu,‡ Ranjit Mishra,‡ Tanmay Bhowmik and Sudip Barman *

 Design and synthesis of HER/HOR catalysts are of crucial importance for the development of polymer fuel
 cells and water electrolyzers. We report the synthesis of Rh–Rh2O3 nanoparticles/nitrogen-doped carbon
 composite (Rh–Rh2O3-NPs/C) for HER/HOR applications. The HER activity of this catalyst is 2.2 times and
 1.43 times better than that of commercial Pt/C in base and acid, respectively. Rh–Rh2O3-NPs/C exhibited 10
 mA cm2 current density at an overpotential of 63 mV and 13 mV with Tafel slopes of 70 mV dec1 and
 32 mV dec1 in base and acid, respectively. The catalyst showed superior HOR activity at all pH values.
 The exchange current densities were 0.425 mA cmRh2 and 0.43 mA cmRh2 in base and acid,
 respectively. In base, the HOR and HER activities of Rh–Rh2O3-NPs/C are 50-fold and 10-fold higher,
 respectively, in comparison with those of the Rh2O3-free RhNPs/C catalyst, although the HER/HOR
 activity of both the catalysts is comparable in acid. In base, the adsorption of OH species (OHads) on
 Rh2O3 sites increases the reactivity of hydrogen intermediate (Habs), which leads to the enhancement of
 Received 10th August 2018
 Accepted 24th October 2018
 HOR activity of Rh–Rh2O3-NPs/C. For HER in base, the adsorptive dissociation of water occurs on the
 Rh2O3 sites to form Hads on the neighboring Rh sites and then, the recombination of Hads results in the
 DOI: 10.1039/c8ta07028h
 formation of hydrogen molecules. This study may provide an opportunity to develop an eﬃcient catalyst
 rsc.li/materials-a for hydrogen-based renewable energy technologies.

 of Rh–Rh–Rh2O3-NPs/C shows strong proton adsorption–
 desorption peaks in 0.5 M H2SO4 solution. A broad anodic peak
 at E z 0.75 V corresponds to the formation of Rh–O, and its
 corresponding cathodic peak located at 0.52 V is ascribed to the
 reduction of Rh–O. The symmetrical cathodic and anodic peaks
 at 0.09 V and 0.12 V are assigned to UPD hydrogen adsorption
 (UPD-Hads) and desorption (UPD-Hdes) from the Rh–Rh2O3-NPs/
 C surface, respectively. The calculated DEp value for UPD-H of
 the Rh–Rh2O3-NPs/C composite was 30 mV, which is lower

 than the reversible value of 60 mV. Recently, Gasteiger et al.

 towards HER in basic media. Tafel slope is an inherent property 33 mV dec1. This suggests that the HER in acidic medium
 of a catalyst. The HER Tafel plot is presented in Fig. 3e. The follows the Volmer–Tafel pathway, where the Tafel pathway is
 Tafel slope of Rh–Rh2O3-NPs/C in 0.5 M KOH solution was
 70 mV dec1, which was lower than that of comm. Pt/C (113 mV
 dec1) and comm. Rh/C (116 mV dec1). This low Tafel slope
 value indicates that the Rh–Rh2O3-NPs/C catalyst follows
 Volmer–Heyrovsky pathway, where the Heyrovsky pathway is
 the rate-limiting step. The exchange current density (i0) is also
 an important kinetic parameter that reveals the rate of electron
 transfer at the reversible condition. The i0 values of Rh–Rh2O3-
 NPs/C, comm. Pt/C and comm. Rh/C were 1.5 mA cm2, 1.3 mA
 cm2 and 0.9 mA cm2, respectively, in 0.5 M KOH medium.

 higher than that in acidic solutions. The exchange current catalyst gradually decreases (oxophilicity increases) with the
 increase in pH of the solution. Its HOR activity also gradually
 decreases with the increase in pH of the solution. However, HBE
 of RhNPs/C catalyst increases with the increase in pH of the
 solution. Hence, HBE in the basic medium can explain the poor
 HOR activity of the RhNPs/C catalyst. Moreover, the presence of
 Rh2O3 in Rh–Rh2O3-NPs/C catalyst facilitates OH adsorption,
 and it has stronger OH adsorption at all pH values than that of
 RhNPs/C. However, the increase in OH adsorption on the Rh–
 Rh2O3-NPs/C catalyst is small at solutions with pH above 7. Rh–
 Rh2O3-NPs/C also exhibited very less pH dependent/
 independent HOR activity. This suggests that the oxophilicity
 of the catalyst (Rh–Rh2O3-NPs/C) has played a signicant role in
 enhancing the HOR activity in basic medium. The strain
 introduced by Rh2O3 on Rh metal alters the electronic structure
 of the catalyst. The presence of Rh2O3 in Rh–Rh2O3-NPs/C
 lowers the HBE of the catalyst due to the electronic eﬀect and
 also enhances the OH adsorption (oxophilic character) of the
 Rh–Rh2O3-NPs/C catalyst. Based on above observations, we
 proposed a bi-functional mechanism of Rh–Rh2O3-NPs/C cata-
 lyst for its enhanced HOR activity in basic media. Fig. 8a shows
 a schematic of HOR mechanism in alkaline medium. Rh metal
 is a good catalyst for the hydrogen intermediate (Hads), whereas

 The superior activity and stability of this catalyst could be
 attributed to several other following reasons.
 One important factor could be the synergistic eﬀect of the
 three components in the Rh–Rh2O3-NPs/C hybrid. Each of the
 three components has diﬀerent functions: Rh metal and Rh2O3
 serve as active sites for H adsorption and OH adsorption,
 respectively, whereas the supported carbon material acts as
 a high electrical conductive support required for electro-
 catalysis. The high activity could be also due to the strong
